title: Every Person Must Be Able to Get In, Move Around and Get Out
summary: Egress is the code's answer to one question: can everyone reach safety before conditions become dangerous? Accessibility asks a second: can everyone, including people with disabilities, reach and use the building at all? Both are geometry fixed early in design, and both are very expensive to fix after the walls are built.
body:
A building must let every person get in, move around and get out. Egress is the code's route to safety in an emergency; accessibility is the route to use on an ordinary day. Both are decided by geometry at concept stage, and both are among the most expensive things to correct once the structure is built.

Recall

Q. Which code edition generally governs a project?

A. The adopted edition, with local amendments, in force when a complete permit application is filed, subject to local transition rules.

Q. What is the design flood elevation?

A. The flood level the design actually uses: the base flood elevation plus required freeboard and any owner margin, measured from a stated datum.

Q. What is a family constitution, in concept?

A. A written statement of a family's shared values, decision rules and roles for owning assets together across generations. It is usually not a legal contract on its own; legal effect comes from the documents that implement it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, stairs, corridors and accessible routes take floor area you cannot sell, and they fix the shape of every floor plate. If they are wrong, they are wrong in concrete. A fire that traps people is the worst outcome a developer can be part of, and an inaccessible building invites complaints, lawsuits and retrofit orders that can arrive years after you sold. This week Cyrus teaches both, using the International Building Code (IBC) and the American accessibility standards it references.

The means of egress has three parts

In plain English: the way out is a path from wherever you are, to a protected way out, to the open air.

The professional framing is the means of egress: a continuous, unobstructed path of travel from any occupied point in a building to a public way. The IBC divides it into three parts [unverified — confirm independently]. The exit access is the part you walk through to reach an exit: rooms, corridors, aisles. The exit is the protected part, separated from the rest of the building by fire-rated construction, such as an enclosed stair or a door directly outside. The exit discharge carries people from the end of the exit to a public way such as a street. Each part has rules for width, length, protection and lighting.

Distance and number are the two big limits

Travel distance is how far a person must walk from the most remote point to the entrance of the nearest exit. The code limits it by occupancy, with longer distances allowed in sprinklered buildings [unverified — confirm independently]. A related limit, the common path of egress travel, caps how far a person may walk before they have a choice of two separate ways out. And the code requires a minimum number of exits, rising with the number of occupants on a floor, with the exits placed far enough apart that one fire is unlikely to block both [unverified — confirm independently].

Worked example 1, hypothetical. A corridor-loaded residential floor is 300 feet long with one stair at each end. A unit door in the middle is 150 feet from either stair, plus the walk inside the unit to its door, say 40 feet: 190 feet. Suppose the adopted code allows 250 feet in a sprinklered building of this occupancy; this figure is for the exercise and must be confirmed [unverified — confirm independently]. The floor works. Now the architect proposes moving one stair inward to free a corner unit with a view. The remote end unit becomes 260 feet from the nearest stair. It fails, and you also create a dead-end corridor, a stretch where people can travel in only one direction, which the code limits in length. A view gained, a code limit lost: that trade must be seen at concept.

Say that out loud now.

Exit access, exit, exit discharge: and the farthest person must reach an exit within the limit.

Accessibility: the route and the room

In plain English: a person using a wheelchair must be able to get from the street to the door, through the door and into the rooms they need to use.

The professional framing is the accessible route: a continuous, unobstructed path that a person with a disability can use, meeting limits on width, slope, cross slope, changes in level, door clearances and turning space. The IBC's accessibility chapter requires accessible routes and a share of accessible units, and refers to ICC A117.1 for the technical details [unverified — confirm independently]. Separately, federal civil rights law applies its own requirements: the Americans with Disabilities Act for public accommodations such as hotels, shops and offices, and the Fair Housing Act design requirements for many multifamily dwellings. Cyrus returns to that legal layer on Day 4.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. The Week 99 flood example put the ground floor 4.8 feet above the street. A 1 in 12 ramp needs about 58 feet of run plus landings. If the only entrance faces a narrow street, the ramp may not fit, and the accessible route must come from another side, or the site must be graded up gradually. Resilience and accessibility collide at the front door, and the collision must be resolved in the same drawing.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners bring an accessibility specialist and an egress review into concept design, not plan review. They draw the accessible route from the public sidewalk to every required unit on the first site plan, and they mark travel distances and dead ends on every floor plan at every stage gate. A small developer can copy this by asking the architect for two overlays on each concept plan: an egress diagram with distances, and an accessible route diagram from the street.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: some jurisdictions offer credits or deductions for removing access barriers; verify that against the primary source. Liability: egress failures can cost lives, and accessibility failures attract civil rights claims that can follow the building after sale. Banking: lenders and their consultants increasingly check accessibility compliance in diligence. Governance: only the owner approves changes that touch stair locations or accessible routes. Estate: an heir inherits exposure to accessibility claims along with the building. Exit: a buyer's diligence may price retrofit costs off your price.

Exits must stay usable for the life of the building

Egress is not finished when the building is. Exit doors get locked for security, corridors fill with storage, exit signs fail and stair doors are propped open, defeating the fire separation that makes the stair an exit. The fire code governs ongoing maintenance of the means of egress after occupancy [unverified — confirm independently]. As owner, put egress inspections into the property manager's routine: monthly walks of every corridor and stair, and a rule that no exit door is locked against people leaving.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating egress and accessibility as details to resolve at plan review, when they are geometry fixed at concept. The control is an egress diagram and an accessible route diagram on every concept plan, reviewed at every stage gate. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect, with an accessibility specialist on any building that serves the public or contains multifamily housing.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a building permit proves accessibility compliance. The building official enforces the building code; federal civil rights requirements can impose obligations the permit did not check.

Callback

In Week 99, Ravi taught that resilience decisions belong in the brief before design. Egress and accessibility belong in the same brief, because the front door, the ramp and the stair cores are where flood, fire and access all have to agree.

Recap

The means of egress runs from exit access through the exit to the exit discharge, within limits on distance and number. Accessibility is a route and a room that a person with a disability can reach and use. Both are geometry; draw them first.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: The Station nightclub fire, and why people head for the door they came in through.
checklist: Ask for an egress diagram with travel distances on every concept floor plan.
Mark the common path of travel and any dead-end corridors.
Confirm the number of exits each floor needs and that they are separated.
Draw the accessible route from the public sidewalk to every required unit and space.
Resolve the flood floor elevation and the accessible entrance in the same drawing.
Identify which federal accessibility laws apply to each part of the building.
Review egress and accessibility at every stage gate.
Get sign-off from a registered architect and an accessibility specialist.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every person must be able to get in, move around and get out. The means of egress has three parts: exit access, the rooms and corridors you walk through; the exit, a protected stair or door outside; and the exit discharge to a public way. The code limits travel distance from the most remote point to the nearest exit, the common path before you have two choices, and dead-end corridors, and it sets the number of exits and how far apart they must be. Moving one stair for a better view can break all three. Accessibility is an accessible route, with limits on width, slope and level changes, from the street to every space and unit that must be accessible, under the building code, ICC A117.1, and federal civil rights law. A permit does not prove civil rights compliance. Both are geometry, so I put an egress diagram and an accessible route diagram on every concept plan.
terms: Means of egress — a continuous, unobstructed path from any occupied point in a building to a public way, made of exit access, exit and exit discharge.
Travel distance — the distance a person must walk from the most remote point to the nearest exit, limited by the code.
Accessible route — a continuous path that a person with a disability can use, meeting limits on width, slope, level changes and clearances.

hostile.q: The architect wants to move a stair to create a premium corner unit. Why are you blocking a revenue gain?
hostile.a: I am not blocking it; I am pricing it. Moving the stair puts the far end units beyond the travel distance limit and creates a dead-end corridor, on the architect's own egress diagram. If we can solve that with another stair or a different layout and the corner unit still earns more than the extra cost, I will approve it. What I will not do is move a stair and discover the egress problem at plan review.

title: The Station Nightclub Fire: The Door They Came In Through
summary: On February 20, 2003, pyrotechnics at The Station nightclub in West Warwick, Rhode Island, ignited flammable foam on the walls, and 100 people died. Many tried to leave through the front entrance they had used to come in, and the crush there blocked it. The case shows that egress design must account for how people actually behave.
body:
On the night of February 20, 2003, The Station nightclub in West Warwick, Rhode Island, filled with smoke in minutes, and 100 people died. The building had other exits. Many people went for the front door, the one they came in through, and the crush there sealed it.

Recall

Q. What are the three parts of a means of egress?

A. Exit access, the path to an exit; the exit, the protected part; and the exit discharge, from the exit to a public way.

Q. What is an adopted edition?

A. The specific edition of a model code that a government has made law, with its local amendments.

Q. Why does a windborne debris region matter?

A. Because windows and doors there must resist impact or be protected, since a broken opening lets wind pressurise the building.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the code gives you rules for width, distance and number of exits. This case shows what those rules exist to protect against, and where a building can meet the letter of a rule and still fail its people. The facts below are the public record as I understand it, drawn largely from the federal investigation by the National Institute of Standards and Technology; verify any detail against that report before you rely on it.

Step 1: The timeline

The Station was a single-storey wood-frame building used as a nightclub. On the night of the fire, a band was playing to a crowd that filled the room. At the start of the set, the band's pyrotechnics, sparks fired from the stage, ignited polyurethane foam that had been fixed to the walls and ceiling around the stage for sound control. The foam burned fast and produced thick, toxic smoke. Within minutes the room was untenable. One hundred people died and many more were injured. The building was not sprinklered.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions stand out. Flammable foam was installed as acoustic treatment. Pyrotechnics were used indoors, close to that foam. And the building was operated as a crowded assembly space without automatic sprinklers. Each decision belonged to different people at different times, which is how layered failures usually form.

Step 3: Assumptions

The assumption behind every egress design is that people will use all the exits available. Research on human behaviour in fires shows otherwise: people tend to leave by the route they know, most often the way they entered, and they move with the crowd. At The Station, many headed for the front entrance, a narrow passage through a vestibule, and the crowd jammed there while other exits were used far less.

Say that out loud now.

People leave by the door they came in through.

Step 4: Incentives

A nightclub earns more with more people inside. Pyrotechnics make a show. Foam is a cheap way to quiet a loud room. None of these incentives is unusual, and none was weighed against the time it takes a crowd to leave a burning room.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Combustible foam on walls was visible to anyone who looked. A crowded room with one obvious main entrance is a known egress risk. An unsprinklered assembly building is a known fire risk. The pattern is familiar from this week: each sign was visible, and nothing connected them into a decision.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once the foam ignited, the fire grew faster than the crowd could leave. In that sense the point of no return was the moment pyrotechnics met foam. In a deeper sense it came earlier, when the room was allowed to operate with fuel on the walls, no sprinklers and an exit layout that relied on people choosing unfamiliar doors.

Step 7: Root cause

For a developer, the root cause is that safety depended on people behaving as the plan assumed, inside a building whose fire load and fire protection gave them almost no time. Egress design that counts exits on paper, without considering which exit people will actually choose, and how fast the room becomes deadly, is incomplete.

What changed afterwards

After the fire, model fire and life safety codes were revised to require sprinklers in many nightclubs and similar assembly occupancies, and to tighten crowd management requirements; verify the current provisions against the adopted editions.

Two worked examples in owner thinking

Worked example 1, hypothetical. You design a ground-floor restaurant of 4,000 square feet in a mixed-use building. The code requires two exits; the architect places the main entrance on the street and a second exit at the back, through the kitchen corridor. Ask: will diners, in smoke, find the back exit? Better: place the second exit where it is visible from the dining room, with signage and a clear path, and make the main entrance wide enough for most of the room to leave through it, because most will try.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. A tenant fitting out the restaurant wants acoustic panels on the ceiling. Your lease should require that finishes meet the interior finish rules of the adopted code, that the tenant submit specifications for approval, and that the landlord can inspect. A clause like that costs nothing to write and could be the difference this case describes.

Time is the currency of egress

Fire engineers think about two clocks. The first is the time people need to leave: to notice the fire, decide to move, choose a route and walk out. The second is the time the building gives them before conditions become deadly: before smoke drops, heat rises or visibility fails. Egress works when the first clock finishes well before the second. Every element of a fire strategy pushes one clock or the other. Wide, visible, familiar exits shorten the first. Sprinklers, low-flammability finishes, smoke control and compartments lengthen the second.

At The Station, the second clock was extraordinarily short because the fuel on the walls burned so fast and there were no sprinklers to slow it, and the first clock was long because so many people chose the same narrow route. Neither clock alone explains the deaths. Together they do. That is why Rule 101 binds the two: you cannot design exits without also designing the time people will have to use them.

What a developer controls

Most developers will never build a nightclub. But every developer builds lobbies, restaurants, amenity rooms, event spaces and retail units, and leases them to operators who will change finishes, add stages, hold events and pack rooms. Your controls sit in three places: in the design, by making exits visible and the main entrance generous; in the specifications, by requiring compliant interior finishes and sprinklers; and in the leases and house rules, by requiring tenant approval for finishes and banning indoor pyrotechnics. The last of the three is the one most often missing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is egress designed to count exits rather than to empty rooms. The control is an egress review that asks which exit people will choose, ensures every exit is visible and usable from the spaces it serves, and pairs egress with sprinklers and controlled interior finishes. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect and a licensed fire protection engineer.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming tenant fit-outs are the tenant's problem. Your building's safety includes what tenants put on its walls.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught that people act on habit and familiarity under pressure. The Station is that lesson at its most serious: in a fire, people do what they already know, and the building must be designed for that.

Recap

Pyrotechnics ignited flammable foam in a crowded, unsprinklered nightclub, smoke filled the room in minutes, and many people jammed the entrance they had come in through. Design egress for real behaviour, and control fuel and fire protection together.

Rule 101: Design every exit route for how people actually behave, with the main entrance sized for most of the room and every other exit visible from the spaces it serves, and never let fire protection or interior finishes erode the time people need to get out.

Next: Sage on The Money: what stairs, corridors and accessible units cost, and what fixing them later costs.
checklist: Assume most occupants will leave by the entrance they used.
Size the main entrance to carry a large share of the occupants.
Make every other exit visible and clearly signed from the spaces it serves.
Pair egress design with automatic sprinklers wherever the adopted code requires or risk justifies.
Require tenant finishes to meet the adopted code's interior finish rules, with landlord approval.
Ban indoor pyrotechnics in leases unless permitted and approved.
Get sign-off from a registered architect and a licensed fire protection engineer.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 101: Design every exit route for how people actually behave, with the main entrance sized for most of the room and every other exit visible from the spaces it serves, and never let fire protection or interior finishes erode the time people need to get out.
speak: On February 20, 2003, at The Station nightclub in West Warwick, Rhode Island, pyrotechnics ignited flammable foam fixed around the stage, and 100 people died. The building was not sprinklered, the foam burned fast with thick smoke, and many people went for the front entrance they had come in through, where the crowd jammed. Other exits were used far less. The lesson for a developer is that egress designed to count exits on paper is incomplete. People leave by the route they know, so the main entrance must carry most of the room and every other exit must be visible from the spaces it serves. And egress only works if fire protection and interior finishes give people time. Rule 101: design exits for real behaviour, size the main entrance for most of the room, and never let finishes or missing sprinklers erode the time to get out.
terms: Assembly occupancy — the code's use group for spaces where people gather, such as restaurants, theatres and clubs.
Interior finish — the exposed surface materials on walls and ceilings, which the code limits for how fast flame spreads across them.
Crowd management — the operational measures, such as trained staff and occupant limits, that help a crowded space empty safely.

hostile.q: Your restaurant has the two exits the code requires. Why are you spending more on the entrance and signs?
hostile.a: Because the code sets a minimum and people do not use exits evenly. In a fire, most diners will head for the door they came in through. I am sizing that entrance to carry most of the room and making the second exit visible from every table. It is a small cost against the one outcome I can never undo.

title: What Stairs, Corridors and Accessible Units Cost
summary: Egress and accessibility take floor area you cannot sell and add cost to units, but they cost far more when fixed after construction. Price them as efficiency, as unit mix and as retrofit risk, and treat compliance as part of the asset's value rather than a deduction from it.
body:
Every stair, corridor and accessible unit is a cost you can see on day one. A missing one is a cost you see later, at several times the price, plus the legal fees. Price egress and accessibility as efficiency, unit mix and retrofit risk, and the case for getting them right at concept makes itself.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 101?

A. Design every exit route for how people actually behave, with the main entrance sized for most of the room and every other exit visible from the spaces it serves, and never let fire protection or interior finishes erode the time people need to get out.

Q. What is the code's tabular allowable area?

A. The area per story the code's table permits for an occupancy and construction type, before increases.

Q. What is expected annual loss?

A. The probability-weighted average yearly cost of a hazard.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors and lenders read your pro forma through efficiency: how much of the gross floor area earns rent or sale value. Egress and accessibility are where efficiency is won or lost, and where a hidden defect can become a lawsuit and a retrofit bill long after you thought the project was finished.

Efficiency is the first price

In plain English: every square foot of stair and corridor is a square foot nobody pays you for.

The professional framing is the efficiency ratio: net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area. Stairs, corridors, elevator shafts, lobbies and service rooms make up the difference. Egress rules set the minimum number and width of stairs and corridors; design choices decide how much more you spend.

Worked example 1, hypothetical round numbers. A residential floor of 20,000 gross square feet. Two stairs at 300 square feet each, an elevator core of 400, and a double-loaded corridor 6 feet wide by 220 feet long, 1,320 square feet, plus 380 square feet of service rooms: 2,700 square feet of non-saleable area. Efficiency is 17,300 divided by 20,000, which is 86.5 percent. The architect proposes a single-loaded corridor along one side for daylight, doubling the corridor to 2,640 square feet; efficiency falls to 79.9 percent. On 10 floors at a hypothetical 500 dollars per saleable square foot, the 1,320 square feet a floor lost is 6,600,000 dollars of revenue. Daylight in a corridor is not worth that unless the units it serves earn a large premium.

Unit mix is the second price

Accessible units need larger bathrooms, wider doors, clearances in the kitchen and turning space. In many multifamily buildings, a share of units must meet the full accessible standard and most of the rest must meet a less demanding adaptable standard; the exact shares come from the adopted code and federal law and must be confirmed. The cost is mostly area: an accessible bathroom may need 15 to 25 square feet more than a standard one, depending on layout.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. A 100-unit building needs 5 fully accessible units. Each needs 40 extra square feet for bathroom and kitchen clearances. That is 200 square feet, at 500 dollars a saleable square foot equivalent, 100,000 dollars of area, plus perhaps 5,000 dollars per unit in fixtures and fittings, 25,000 dollars. About 125,000 dollars on a building that might cost 30,000,000 dollars: under half of one percent. Designed in from the start, it disappears into the plan. Distributed sensibly across unit types and floors, which the rules often require, these units also sell and lease like any other.

Say that out loud now.

Accessibility designed in is a fraction of a percent; accessibility retrofitted is a project of its own.

Retrofit is the third price

Correcting accessibility after construction means demolishing and rebuilding finished work: moving walls for bathroom clearances, re-sloping walks, widening doors, replacing fixtures, often in occupied units. Claims under federal civil rights law can come from residents, advocacy groups or government enforcement, and can involve legal costs as well as the work itself. The financial pattern is consistent: the retrofit costs many times the original design change, and the legal process adds cost and delay. Verify the enforcement mechanisms and remedies against primary source and with a licensed lawyer.

A rough hypothetical. If the 5 accessible units in worked example 2 were built wrong and had to be rebuilt in occupied condition at, say, 40,000 dollars each, plus resident relocation and professional fees, the correction could approach 300,000 dollars, two to three times the original cost, before any legal fees. Then add the doors, walks and common areas.

Value, not deduction

A buyer or lender's consultant will review accessibility and egress in diligence. A building with a clean compliance record, a consultant's sign-off and as-built drawings is easier to finance and sell. A building with known defects is priced for the retrofit and the risk, and some buyers will walk.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: a civil rights claim can attach to the owner, and some exposures survive a sale or follow the developer who built the building. That makes accessibility part of personal risk, not only project cost. A licensed adviser and lawyer are required before you rely on any structure to limit that exposure.

Egress width bites at the ground floor

Day 5 will show that on residential floors the minimum stair width usually governs, so egress costs there are mostly fixed. The cost of egress concentrates where crowds gather: restaurants, amenity rooms, event spaces and retail. A ground-floor tenant that wants a high occupant load may need wider doors, a second exit that consumes frontage, or larger exit corridors through the building to the street. Each of those can reduce leasable area or valuable street frontage.

Worked example 3, hypothetical. A landlord leases a 5,000-square-foot ground-floor unit to a restaurant at 60 dollars per square foot a year, 300,000 dollars. The restaurant's occupant load requires a second exit through the building to a side street, taking 400 square feet of a neighbouring retail unit that leases at 40 dollars, 16,000 dollars a year. At a 7 percent capitalisation rate, that lost rent is about 228,000 dollars of value. Planned at concept, the exit corridor can be placed where it costs least, perhaps behind back-of-house space. Discovered when the restaurant signs, it lands wherever it fits, and the landlord pays.

The practical move is simple: decide at concept which ground-floor units are designed for high-occupancy tenants, give those units the exits they need from the start, and price the rents accordingly. A restaurant-ready unit with its exits, grease duct route and sprinkler capacity built in commands better tenants and leases faster than a shell that must be rebuilt for them.

Put all three prices in one table at concept: efficiency by floor, accessible unit cost, and a retrofit estimate for the same items. Investors who see the third column rarely ask to cut the first two.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is squeezing efficiency by trimming corridor widths, bathroom clearances or ramp lengths below what the rules require. The control is an accessibility review of every floor and unit type at each design stage, with sign-off required from a registered architect and an accessibility specialist.

The beginner's mistake

Counting accessible units as a cost and stopping. They are also units that sell and lease, to a market that is larger than many developers assume.

Callback

In Week 16, Sage taught that a buyer's appraiser and diligence team price risk into value. Accessibility defects are exactly the risk they price, so getting them right is protecting the exit cap rate as well as the cost line.

Recap

Price egress and accessibility as efficiency, unit mix and retrofit risk. Designed in, they cost a fraction of a percent; retrofitted, they cost several times as much plus legal fees. Treat compliance as value.

Next: Cyrus on The Rules: the building code, the accessibility standard and the federal civil rights laws that sit beside them.
checklist: Calculate efficiency for every concept floor plate.
Price any design choice that lowers efficiency in lost saleable area.
Confirm the required share of fully accessible and adaptable units with the architect.
Distribute accessible units across unit types and floors as the rules require.
Price accessibility at design stage and compare with a retrofit estimate.
Keep accessibility sign-off and as-built drawings for diligence.
Get sign-off from a registered architect and an accessibility specialist.
head: Field checklist
speak: Egress and accessibility have three prices. First, efficiency: stairs, corridors, cores and service rooms are area nobody pays for. On a hypothetical 20,000-square-foot floor, a single-loaded corridor can drop efficiency from about 86 to 80 percent, which on ten floors is millions of dollars of revenue. Second, unit mix: accessible units need larger bathrooms, wider doors and clearances, but on a 100-unit building five accessible units might cost about 125,000 dollars, well under one percent, if designed in. Third, retrofit: rebuilding wrong units in occupied condition can cost two to three times the original, before legal fees, and civil rights claims can follow the owner. A clean compliance record protects financing and sale value. So I design it in, review every unit type at every stage, and keep the sign-off for diligence.
terms: Efficiency ratio — net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area.
Fully accessible unit — a dwelling unit built to the full technical accessibility standard, for example for wheelchair users.
Adaptable unit — a dwelling unit built with basic accessible features so it can be adapted, under a less demanding standard.

hostile.q: Your corridor widths and bathroom sizes are generous. Why not trim them to raise efficiency?
hostile.a: Because they are at the minimum the accessibility rules require, not generous. Trimming them would make units non-compliant, and a retrofit in occupied units would cost several times the area we would gain, plus legal exposure. Where we can gain efficiency, in service rooms and the core layout, the architect is already working on it.

title: Two Layers of Law: The Building Code and Civil Rights
summary: Accessibility in the United States sits in two layers: the building code enforced by the building official, and federal civil rights laws enforced by complaints, lawsuits and government agencies. A building can pass one and fail the other. Then compare, conceptually, how Canada and Guyana approach the same idea.
body:
Accessibility law has two layers. The building code is checked by the building official before you occupy. Federal civil rights law, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Fair Housing Act, applies whether or not anyone checked, and it is enforced after the fact. Design to both, because passing one does not prove the other.

Recall

Q. What is the efficiency ratio?

A. Net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area.

Q. What does the building official's authority over alternative methods allow?

A. Approval of designs not specifically prescribed by the code where equivalence is demonstrated, usually by an engineer's analysis.

Q. What is an exit discharge?

A. The part of the means of egress between the end of an exit and a public way.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, many owners believe that a certificate of occupancy closes the accessibility question. It closes the building code question for the code that was checked. The civil rights layer can open years later through a complaint, and the owner, and sometimes the designer and builder, must answer it. Knowing which layer governs which part of your building tells you whom to hire and what to keep.

Layer one: the building code

In plain English: the building code sets accessibility rules the building official checks at plan review and inspection.

The IBC's accessibility chapter sets where accessible routes, entrances, parking and units are required, and how many, and it refers to ICC A117.1 for technical criteria such as clear widths, turning spaces, reach ranges and fixture heights [unverified — confirm independently]. Egress rules in the same code require accessible means of egress, which can include areas of refuge where people who cannot use stairs wait for assistance, protected and with communication to the outside [unverified — confirm independently]. Enforcement is through the permit: plan review, inspections and the certificate of occupancy.

Layer two: federal civil rights law

In plain English: federal law makes discrimination against people with disabilities unlawful, and for buildings that means certain physical access.

The Americans with Disabilities Act applies, among other things, to public accommodations, such as hotels, restaurants, shops and offices open to the public, and to commercial facilities. New construction and alterations must meet the federal accessibility standards issued under the Act; those standards are similar to the building code's but not identical. The Fair Housing Act applies design and construction requirements to many multifamily dwellings built for first occupancy after its requirements took effect, covering features such as an accessible building entrance on an accessible route, accessible common areas, usable doors, and accessible features inside covered units [unverified — confirm independently]. The thresholds for which buildings and units are covered, and the dates, must be verified against primary source.

Enforcement differs from the code. There is no plan review for civil rights compliance in most cases. Claims can be brought by individuals, advocacy organisations and federal agencies, and remedies can include orders to retrofit, damages and fees. Verify the enforcement mechanisms and remedies against primary source and with a licensed lawyer.

Say that out loud now.

A permit checks the code; civil rights law applies whether anyone checked or not.

Where the layers meet in one building

Worked example 1, hypothetical. A mixed-use building has ground-floor shops, a short-stay residential floor and condominium floors above. The shops are public accommodations and commercial space under the Act. The short-stay floor, if it is a place of lodging, is subject to the Act's transient lodging requirements, including accessible guest rooms with specific bathing features. The condominium floors are covered multifamily dwellings under the Fair Housing Act design requirements. All three are also under the building code. One building, three civil rights regimes and one code: your accessibility specialist maps which applies to each floor.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. A site plan shows an accessible route from the parking lot to the entrance, but the route crosses a 3-inch curb with no curb ramp because a late landscaping change added a planting bed. The building official misses it at inspection. Two years later, a resident files a complaint. The fix is cheap, perhaps 8,000 dollars for a curb ramp and regrading, but the legal response, the investigation and any settlement cost far more than the ramp. A final walk of every accessible route, with a tape and a level, before you accept the building would have caught it.

Two Systems

Canada, in concept: accessibility requirements for buildings sit largely in the national model building code as adopted, with provincial variations, while human rights legislation at federal and provincial levels prohibits discrimination, and some provinces have separate accessibility statutes with standards and timelines. Guyana, in concept: there is national legislation on the rights of persons with disabilities, and building approvals run through planning and building authorities, with the detailed technical standard to be confirmed for each project. Treat both descriptions as conceptual and verify against primary source.

Who is responsible

Under federal civil rights law, responsibility for design and construction requirements can extend beyond the owner. Claims may be brought against those who design and construct covered buildings, as well as owners, depending on the law and the facts [unverified — confirm independently]. That means your architect, your contractor and you can all be named, and the contracts between you decide who ultimately pays. Your design contract should require the architect to design to the building code and to the applicable federal accessibility standards, named specifically, and your construction contract should require the contractor to build to the drawings and report any conflict it notices. Verify the allocation with a licensed lawyer.

Alterations and existing buildings

When you buy an existing building and alter it, accessibility obligations attach to the work you do. In concept, altered areas must generally meet the standards to the extent feasible, and some laws also require that the path of travel to an altered primary function area be made accessible, subject to a cost proportion limit [unverified — confirm independently]. Separately, public accommodations may have an ongoing duty to remove barriers in existing facilities where that is readily achievable [unverified — confirm independently]. Those concepts change how you budget a repositioning: the accessibility cost is not only what you choose to fix but also what the alterations trigger. Ask your accessibility specialist to scope it before you buy.

Keep the evidence

Because civil rights claims arrive after the fact, your defence is a record. Keep the accessibility specialist's reviews at each design stage, the code basis listing every standard and edition, the field verification measurements, photographs of routes, ramps and key bathroom clearances, and the as-built drawings. Store them with the permit and the certificate of occupancy, and hand a copy to the buyer or the association on sale. A claim that meets a complete, dated record is a much smaller claim.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating the certificate of occupancy as proof of accessibility compliance. The control is an accessibility specialist's review mapping each part of the building to the code and to each civil rights regime, plus a final field verification of routes, units and common areas. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect and an accessibility specialist, with a licensed lawyer for which civil rights regimes apply.

The beginner's mistake

Designing to one standard and assuming the others match. They overlap heavily but differ in details, and the stricter one governs each detail.

Callback

In Week 100, REGA taught that the adopted code, not the model text, governs. Accessibility adds a second axis: the adopted code and the federal standards, each with its own edition and scope. List both in the code basis.

Recap

Accessibility has two layers: the building code, enforced by permit, and federal civil rights law, enforced by complaint. Map every part of the building to both, design to the stricter detail, and verify in the field before you accept the building.

Next: Cyrus on The Numbers: occupant load, number of exits and exit width, step by step.
checklist: Map every floor and space to the building code and to each civil rights regime that applies.
List the federal accessibility standards and their editions beside the adopted code in the code basis.
Design each detail to the stricter of the overlapping standards.
Confirm Fair Housing Act coverage for multifamily floors with a licensed lawyer.
Check transient lodging requirements for any short-stay floor.
Walk every accessible route with a tape and a level before accepting the building.
Keep accessibility reviews and field verification records with the as-builts.
Get sign-off from a registered architect and an accessibility specialist.
head: Field checklist
speak: Accessibility has two layers of law. The building code, through its accessibility chapter and ICC A117.1, is checked by the building official at plan review and inspection, and it includes accessible means of egress. Federal civil rights law sits beside it: the Americans with Disabilities Act for public accommodations and commercial facilities, including hotels, and the Fair Housing Act design requirements for many multifamily dwellings. Those apply whether or not anyone checked, and they are enforced by complaints, lawsuits and agencies, with retrofit orders, damages and fees. A certificate of occupancy does not prove civil rights compliance. In one mixed-use building, shops, short-stay rooms and condominiums can fall under three different regimes and the code. So my accessibility specialist maps every floor to every regime, we design to the stricter detail, and I walk every route with a tape and a level before accepting the building.
terms: Public accommodation — a business open to the public, such as a hotel, restaurant or shop, covered by federal disability rights law.
Area of refuge — a protected space where people who cannot use stairs can wait for assistance during an emergency.
Covered multifamily dwelling — a dwelling unit in a building subject to federal fair housing design and construction requirements.

hostile.q: You have a certificate of occupancy. Why are you paying an accessibility specialist after construction?
hostile.a: Because the certificate shows the building official accepted the building code items they checked. Federal civil rights requirements apply independently and are enforced by complaint, and a missed curb or a bathroom clearance can cost far more to defend than to fix. The specialist's field verification lets us correct anything now, document compliance and protect the sale.

title: Occupant Load, Exits and Exit Width, Step by Step
summary: Egress arithmetic runs in a fixed order: area to occupant load, occupant load to number of exits, occupant load to required width, then a travel distance check. Every factor below is invented for the exercise; the real ones come from the adopted code. The method is the lesson.
body:
Egress arithmetic runs in a fixed order: floor area gives occupant load, occupant load gives the number of exits and their total width, and the plan gives travel distance. Every factor below is invented for this exercise and labelled so; the method is what you need.

Recall

Q. What are the two layers of accessibility law?

A. The building code, enforced by permit, and federal civil rights law, enforced by complaints, lawsuits and agencies.

Q. What is an adaptable unit?

A. A dwelling unit built with basic accessible features so it can be adapted, under a less demanding standard than a fully accessible unit.

Q. What is a dead-end corridor?

A. A stretch of corridor from which people can travel in only one direction to reach an exit, limited in length by the code.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an architect will tell you how many stairs a floor needs and how wide they must be. You should be able to check the logic yourself, because those numbers decide your core, your efficiency and the size of every ground-floor space that holds a crowd.

Step 1: Occupant load

In plain English: the code estimates how many people a space can hold from its area and its use.

The occupant load is the floor area divided by an occupant load factor, a number of square feet per person that the code sets for each use [unverified — confirm independently]. Crowded uses such as dining get small factors, meaning many people; residential uses get large ones. Gross or net area may apply depending on the use. Round up.

Worked example 1, a hypothetical ground-floor restaurant of 5,000 square feet, not your project. Suppose, for this exercise only, the factor is 15 square feet per person for the dining area of 3,600 square feet and 200 square feet per person for the kitchen of 1,400 square feet. Dining: 3,600 divided by 15 is 240 people. Kitchen: 1,400 divided by 200 is 7. Total occupant load: 247 people. These factors are invented.

Step 2: Number of exits

The code requires at least a minimum number of exits or exit access doorways, rising with the occupant load [unverified — confirm independently]. Suppose, for the exercise, that up to 500 occupants need 2. The restaurant needs 2. They must also be separated: a common rule places them at least a set fraction of the space's diagonal apart, so a single fire is unlikely to block both [unverified — confirm independently]. On a room 100 feet by 50 feet, the diagonal is the square root of 100 squared plus 50 squared, about 112 feet. If the rule were one half of the diagonal in this invented case, the exits must be at least 56 feet apart.

Say that out loud now.

Area gives load, load gives number and width, plan gives distance.

Step 3: Exit width

Required width is the occupant load times a width factor in inches per person, with one factor for stairs and a smaller one for doors and level paths, often reduced where the building is sprinklered and has an emergency voice alarm [unverified — confirm independently]. Then a minimum clear width for each door or stair applies, whichever is larger.

Continue the example. Suppose the factor is 0.2 inches per person for doors, invented for this exercise. 247 times 0.2 is 49.4 inches of total door width. Across 2 exits, about 25 inches each, but every exit door also needs a minimum clear width, say 32 inches, so each must be at least 32. And the code usually requires that losing any one exit still leaves a share of the capacity available [unverified — confirm independently]. Remember Rule 101: most diners will use the front door. Sizing the main entrance to carry, say, two-thirds of the room means 247 times two-thirds, about 165 people, times 0.2, which is 33 inches: a single 36-inch leaf works, but a pair of doors is better for a crowd.

Step 4: Travel distance and common path

Worked example 2, the residential floor above, hypothetical. The corridor is 240 feet with a stair at each end. The farthest point inside a unit is 35 feet from its door, and the unit door is 120 feet from either stair along the corridor. Travel distance is 155 feet. Suppose the limit for this sprinklered residential use is 250 feet, invented for this exercise. It passes with 95 feet to spare.

Now check the common path: from the farthest point in the unit to the point in the corridor where the occupant can turn either way toward two stairs. That is 35 feet in the unit plus the corridor distance from the door to that choice point, here zero, because the door opens onto a corridor with stairs in both directions. If a unit sat at a corridor end beyond the last stair, the walk back to the stair would count against the dead-end limit instead.

Step 5: Stair width on the residential floor

A residential floor of 20,000 gross square feet with an invented factor of 200 square feet per person holds 100 occupants. With an invented stair factor of 0.3 inches per person, required total stair width is 30 inches, far below a typical minimum stair width of 44 inches for this kind of occupant load [unverified — confirm independently]. So the minimum width governs, not the arithmetic. That is common in residential buildings, and it is why the restaurant, not the apartments, is usually where egress width bites.

The table you check

ItemRestaurantResidential floor
Occupant load247100
Exits required22
Width by factor49 inches30 inches
Governing widthFactor and main door shareMinimum width

Worked example 3: accessible means of egress

Egress arithmetic does not end with stairs. People who cannot use stairs need an accessible means of egress: an accessible route to an exit, and on upper floors usually an area of refuge or another approved arrangement, such as an elevator designed for evacuation where permitted [unverified — confirm independently]. Suppose, invented for this exercise, that each area of refuge on a residential floor needs space for one wheelchair, about 30 by 48 inches, outside the required stair width. That is 10 square feet per stair per floor. On two stairs over 10 floors, 200 square feet. Small, but it must be drawn into the stair landing at concept or it will push the stair wider later. In a sprinklered building, the adopted code may relax some of these requirements; confirm with your code consultant.

The lesson is the same as the rest of the week: the number is small when you plan it and large when you discover it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is using invented or remembered factors, like the ones above, in a real decision. The control is a code consultant's egress calculation using the adopted edition's factors, shown on the drawings for every space. Professional sign-off required: a registered architect.

The beginner's mistake

Calculating the occupant load the operator hopes for rather than the one the code assigns. The code load governs exits, plumbing fixture counts and sometimes sprinkler and alarm requirements.

Callback

In Week 100, Ivo reverse engineered a floor plate from the area the code allows. Egress is the same discipline in the other direction: the area you draw produces an occupant load, and the load produces the stairs and doors you must build.

Recap

Area divided by factor gives occupant load; load gives number of exits and width by factor, subject to minimums; the plan gives travel distance and common path. Use only adopted factors, and size the main entrance for how people really leave.

Next: Marco in The Room: the design review where the accessibility consultant finds the unit bathrooms are wrong.
checklist: Calculate occupant load for every space from area and the adopted factor.
Confirm the number of exits each space and floor needs.
Check exit separation against the diagonal rule in the adopted code.
Calculate required width by factor and compare with minimum widths.
Size the main entrance for the share of occupants who will use it.
Check travel distance, common path and dead ends on every floor.
Use only the adopted edition's factors, with a code consultant's calculation.
head: Field checklist
speak: Egress arithmetic runs in a fixed order. First, occupant load: area divided by the code's occupant load factor for each use, rounded up. In my invented example, a 5,000-square-foot restaurant holds 247 people. Second, number of exits: the code sets a minimum by load, here two, separated by a set fraction of the room's diagonal so one fire cannot block both. Third, width: load times a width factor in inches per person, then compare with each door's minimum clear width; I also size the main entrance for the two-thirds of the room that will use it. Fourth, travel distance and common path on every floor. On a residential floor the minimum stair width usually governs, so the restaurant is where width bites. Every factor I used was invented; the real ones come from the adopted code and a code consultant's calculation.
terms: Occupant load — the number of people the code assumes a space can hold, from its area and use.
Occupant load factor — the code's floor area per person for a use, used to calculate occupant load.
Common path of egress travel — the distance an occupant must travel before having a choice of two separate routes to exits.

hostile.q: The operator says the restaurant will never hold more than 150 people. Why are you building exits for 247?
hostile.a: Because the code assigns the occupant load from area and use, not from the operator's forecast, and that load governs the exits, the plumbing fixtures and the fire protection. If we wanted to build for 150, we would have to reduce the dining area or post and enforce a lower load under the adopted code, and our code consultant would have to confirm that route. Until then, we build for 247.

title: The Design Review Where the Bathrooms Are Wrong
summary: An accessibility consultant reports that the unit bathrooms do not meet the required clearances, and the contractor is ready to start framing. Learn how to run that meeting: the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to keep the schedule without accepting a defect.
body:
The cheapest moment to fix an accessibility defect is before the walls are framed, and it is also the moment when everyone wants to keep going. Your job in this meeting is to stop the defect, not the project.

Recall

Q. How do you calculate occupant load?

A. Divide the floor area by the adopted code's occupant load factor for the use, and round up.

Q. Why does a certificate of occupancy not prove civil rights compliance?

A. Because it covers the building code items the official checked, while federal civil rights law applies independently and is enforced by complaint.

Q. What is a pre-application meeting for?

A. To hear the building department's reading of the code basis before design is complete, so the design follows it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will run meetings like this one as owner. The facts will be technical, the schedule will be tight, and the contractor and the architect will each have reasons for the problem to belong to someone else. The way you run it decides whether the fix costs a redesign or a retrofit.

The scene

This is a hypothetical building, not your project. Framing of the residential floors starts in two weeks. Your accessibility consultant, hired late, has reviewed the unit drawings and reports that the bathrooms in two unit types, about 40 units, do not provide the clear floor space required at the toilet and the turning space required by the adaptable standard, and that 3 fully accessible units have doors that swing into the required clear space. Present: the architect, the contractor's project manager and superintendent, the consultant, and Marco, running the meeting for you.

The question behind the question

The contractor is asking: will this delay my framing, and who pays? The architect is asking: is this my error, and will it be on the record? Your question is: what is the smallest correct fix, and can it be made before framing starts?

The lines to say

"Thank you for finding this before framing. That is the best possible timing."

"Let us agree the facts first. Is the consultant's reading of the standard correct?" Then ask the architect directly, and listen.

"What is the smallest layout change that makes these bathrooms compliant, and how many square feet does it cost each unit?"

"Can framing start on the unaffected floors or unit types while the revised layouts are issued?"

"We will deal with responsibility and cost separately, in writing. Today we fix the design."

Say that out loud now.

Today we fix the design; responsibility comes later, in writing.

The lines never to say

Never say "Can we build it as drawn and fix it later?" Fixing finished bathrooms costs many times more, and building a known defect is a decision you would have to defend. Never say "Nobody will ever check." Civil rights law is enforced by complaint, often years later. Never blame the architect in front of the contractor; it damages the relationship you need for every remaining drawing, and it prejudges a question that belongs in a separate, written process. And never let the consultant's finding go unanswered in the minutes.

When to stay silent

After you ask the architect whether the consultant is right, stop talking. A professional who says "yes, we missed it" in a calm room will fix it quickly. A professional who feels cornered will argue the standard, and you will lose a week.

Two worked exchanges

Worked example 1, hypothetical. The architect agrees and proposes swapping the vanity and toilet positions and changing the door to swing out, recovering the clear space within the same footprint in one unit type. In the other, the bathroom must grow by 12 square feet, taken from a closet. Cost: redesign fees and no extra area on the first type; on the second, 20 units times 12 square feet, 240 square feet of closet space lost, which the sales team says does not change the price. You approve both, subject to the consultant's sign-off on the revised layouts.

Worked example 2, hypothetical. The contractor says revised drawings will delay framing by two weeks. You ask the superintendent which floors and unit types are unaffected. He says three floors can start on schedule because the affected types sit higher in the building. Framing starts on time; the revised drawings arrive before the crews reach the affected floors. Delay: zero. Had the defect been built, a retrofit of 40 bathrooms in finished condition at a hypothetical 12,000 dollars each would have cost 480,000 dollars.

Holding your state

You may feel anger that the problem exists at all, and pressure from the schedule. Neither helps. Breathe slowly before you speak, keep your voice level, and keep the meeting on facts and fixes. The calm owner who says "thank you for finding this" makes the next problem more likely to be reported early.

After the meeting

Within a day, issue a note: the finding, the agreed fix for each unit type, the sign-off required from the consultant, the floors that proceed, and the date of revised drawings. Separately, write to the architect asking how the error occurred and how their quality control will prevent another. Keep the cost discussion for later, once the facts are settled.

The cost conversation, later

A week after the meeting, when the revised drawings are issued and signed off, take up the cost. Ask the architect for a written account of the error and the time spent fixing it. Look at the design contract: if it required compliance with the applicable accessibility standards and the drawings did not comply, the redesign is generally within the architect's own scope rather than an additional service, though your contract decides. Ask the contractor for any genuine cost of resequencing, with evidence. Most of these conversations end amicably when the problem was found early and fixed fast, because the sums are small. They end badly when the problem was hidden and built.

Keep a short record of the whole episode: the finding, the fix, the sign-off, the cost and who bore it. If a resident ever raises a complaint about those units, the record shows the owner found the issue, fixed it before construction and verified the result, which is exactly the evidence of care you want.

Prevention for the next project

Three changes stop this happening again. Hire the accessibility consultant at schematic design. Make their sign-off a condition of each design stage gate. And ask the architect to include an accessibility checklist in their own quality control, with each unit type checked against it before any drawing is issued.

And thank the consultant again, in writing, copied to the team. The message you want everyone to hear is that finding problems early is rewarded on your projects.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is building a known accessibility defect to protect the schedule. The control is a rule that no unit type is framed until its layout carries the accessibility consultant's sign-off. Professional sign-off required: the registered architect of record and the accessibility specialist.

The beginner's mistake

Hiring the accessibility consultant after the drawings are complete. The best review happens at schematic design, when a layout change costs a sketch.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught independent review: a reviewer outside the design team who checks the work before it is relied on. The accessibility consultant is that reviewer, and a sign-off before framing turns the review into a hold point: work does not pass it until the check is done.

Recap

Thank the finder, agree the facts, find the smallest correct fix, keep unaffected work moving, separate fixing from blame, and never build a known defect.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on egress and accessibility, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: Thank whoever found the defect, in the meeting.
Agree the facts with the architect before discussing fixes.
Ask for the smallest layout change that makes each unit type compliant.
Keep unaffected floors and unit types moving.
Separate the design fix from responsibility and cost, in writing.
Require the accessibility consultant's sign-off on revised layouts before framing.
Issue a meeting note within a day.
head: Field checklist
speak: When the accessibility consultant finds the bathrooms are wrong two weeks before framing, I thank them first, because that is the best possible timing. I ask the architect, calmly, whether the reading is correct, and then I stay silent. We look for the smallest correct fix for each unit type, often swapping fixtures and changing a door swing within the same footprint, sometimes taking a few square feet from a closet. I ask the superintendent which floors and unit types are unaffected so framing starts on time while revised drawings are issued. I never say build it as drawn and fix it later, and I never say nobody will check, because civil rights law is enforced by complaint. Responsibility and cost are handled later, in writing. No unit type is framed until its layout carries the consultant's sign-off.
terms: Clear floor space — the unobstructed area required at a fixture or control so a wheelchair user can approach and use it.
Turning space — the unobstructed area required for a wheelchair to turn around.
Quality control — the designer's or builder's own internal checks that work meets the requirements before it is issued or built.

hostile.q: Fixing these layouts delays my framing. Why not build as drawn and adjust later?
hostile.a: Because adjusting finished bathrooms would cost several times more and would mean knowingly building a defect. We will not lose your start: three floors are unaffected and framing begins there on schedule, and the revised layouts for the affected types arrive before your crews reach them. If there is a real delay cost, put it in writing and we will deal with it separately.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 101 Review: Getting In, Moving Around, Getting Out
summary: Six questions test the week: the parts of a means of egress, travel distance and exits, real human behaviour in fires, the two layers of accessibility law, occupant load arithmetic and the cost of retrofit. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical egress and accessibility memo. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: every person must be able to get in, move around and get out, so draw the exits and accessible routes first, size them for how people really behave, and design to both the building code and civil rights law.

Recall

Q. What should you say first when a consultant finds a defect before construction?

A. Thank them, because finding it before the work is built is the best possible timing.

Q. What does the occupant load govern?

A. The number and width of exits, and often plumbing fixture counts and some fire protection requirements.

Q. What is Rule 99?

A. Treat any engineer's warning that touches structure as a safety decision first and a budget decision second, and design every surface that holds water over structure to drain, be inspected and be replaced.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, egress and accessibility are the part of design that touches every person who ever enters your building. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the three parts of a means of egress.

Answer: Exit access, the path to an exit; the exit, the protected part such as an enclosed stair; and the exit discharge, from the exit to a public way.

Question 2. What does travel distance measure, and what usually increases the limit?

Answer: The distance from the most remote point to the nearest exit; automatic sprinklers usually allow a longer limit under the adopted code.

Question 3. What did The Station fire show about human behaviour?

Answer: People tend to leave by the route they know, often the door they came in through, and they move with the crowd, so exits must be designed for that behaviour.

Question 4. What are the two layers of accessibility law?

Answer: The building code, with ICC A117.1, enforced by permit; and federal civil rights law, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Fair Housing Act, enforced by complaint, lawsuit and agencies.

Question 5. Give the order of egress arithmetic.

Answer: Area divided by the occupant load factor gives load; load gives number of exits and width by factor, subject to minimums; the plan gives travel distance, common path and dead ends.

Question 6. What is Rule 101?

Answer: Design every exit route for how people actually behave, with the main entrance sized for most of the room and every other exit visible from the spaces it serves, and never let fire protection or interior finishes erode the time people need to get out.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Cyrus set out egress and accessibility as geometry. Ford took The Station nightclub fire through seven steps and gave Rule 101. Sage priced efficiency, unit mix and retrofit. Cyrus explained the two layers of accessibility law and compared Canada and Guyana conceptually. Cyrus worked occupant load, exits and width. Marco ran the design review where the bathrooms were wrong.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical memo from a design team to an owner and find the defects before reading on.

Egress and accessibility memo. The ground-floor restaurant has an occupant load of 150, per the operator's estimate, served by the front entrance and a rear exit through the kitchen. Exit widths are at code minimum. The residential stair at the north end has been moved 40 feet south to create a corner unit; travel distances to be checked at plan review. Accessible entrance is via the loading dock. Bathrooms in unit types C and D are compact layouts; accessibility review will follow the permit. ADA compliance is confirmed by the building permit.

The defects. First, the occupant load comes from the operator's estimate, not the adopted code's factor applied to area. Second, the second exit runs through the kitchen, out of sight of diners, which Rule 101 warns against, and the main entrance is not sized for the share of people who will use it. Third, moving the stair without checking travel distance and dead ends pushes a geometry decision to plan review, when it is costly to reverse. Fourth, an accessible entrance through a loading dock is not an equivalent route for the public and is unlikely to satisfy the accessibility rules for a primary entrance. Fifth, compact bathrooms with review deferred until after permit invites a retrofit. Sixth, the claim that the permit confirms ADA compliance confuses the two layers of law. Seventh, no one signed it: no architect, no accessibility specialist.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investor who asks, "Why do the stairs and bathrooms cost us so much area?" Then compare.

Model answer: "Because everyone must be able to get in, move around and get out. The code sets how many stairs each floor needs, how far anyone may walk to one, and how wide the exits must be, from an occupant load the code calculates, not one we choose. We design for how people actually behave in a fire, so the restaurant's main entrance carries most of the room and the second exit is visible. Accessibility sits under the building code and under federal civil rights law, which is enforced by complaint years later, so we design to both and verify in the field. Designed in, the accessible units cost well under one percent of the budget. Retrofitted, they would cost several times that plus legal fees. Our consultant has signed off every unit type before framing."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name both layers of law? Did you give one number? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

Where people go wrong on these questions

On question 1, the slip is to call a corridor an exit. A corridor is usually exit access; the exit is the protected part.

On question 2, people forget the common path and dead-end limits. Travel distance is one of three distance checks.

On question 3, the slip is to say "people panic". Research on fire behaviour shows people more often act rationally on what they know, which is why they head for the familiar door. Design for that.

On question 4, the slip is to say the permit settles it. It settles the code items that were checked.

On question 5, people use the operator's estimate of occupancy. The code's factor governs.

On question 6, practise Rule 101 until you can say it without looking.

Kema's note on practice

Do the boardroom drill twice, once to a mirror and once recorded on your phone, and listen for whether you said "civil rights law" and "building code" as two separate things. Then take the Red Pen memo and, without looking, list the seven defects aloud. If you find five, the week has landed. If you find seven, write one more defect you would add to make the memo harder.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is deferring egress and accessibility review until after design, when the geometry is fixed. The control is egress and accessible route diagrams on every concept plan, and an accessibility specialist's sign-off on every unit type before construction.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the permit as the finish line. Civil rights obligations continue after occupancy.

Callback

In Week 99, Ravi set the ground floor above the design flood elevation, and Cyrus showed on Day 1 that the same decision sets the length of the accessible ramp. A good building resolves flood, fire and access at one front door.

Recap

Egress has three parts and three big limits: distance, number and width. People leave by the door they know. Accessibility lives in two layers of law. Calculate in order, design for behaviour, and sign off before you build.

Next: Magnus on First Principles: the fire strategy, sprinklers, alarms, smoke control and compartments.
checklist: Name the three parts of a means of egress.
What does travel distance measure, and what usually increases the limit?
What did The Station fire show about human behaviour?
What are the two layers of accessibility law?
Give the order of egress arithmetic.
What is Rule 101?
head: The six questions
speak: This week was about getting in, moving around and getting out. The means of egress runs from exit access through a protected exit to the exit discharge, and the code limits travel distance, common path and dead ends, and sets the number and width of exits from an occupant load it calculates from area and use. The Station nightclub fire in 2003 showed that people leave by the door they came in through, so the main entrance must carry most of the room and every other exit must be visible. Accessibility has two layers: the building code with ICC A117.1, enforced by permit, and federal civil rights law, enforced by complaint long after occupancy. Designed in, accessibility costs a fraction of a percent; retrofitted, several times more. Rule 101: design exits for real behaviour and never let finishes or missing sprinklers erode the time to get out.
terms: Public way — a street or other open space permanently available to the public, where the means of egress ends.
Exit separation — the code's requirement that exits be far enough apart that one fire is unlikely to block them all.
Field verification — measuring built work on site to confirm it matches the required dimensions.

hostile.q: Your memo says the permit confirms ADA compliance. Is that true?
hostile.a: No, and I am withdrawing that line. The permit confirms the building official accepted the building code items they reviewed. Federal accessibility requirements apply independently. Our accessibility specialist will map each part of the building to every regime that applies, review the unit layouts before framing and verify the routes in the field, and that record, not the permit, is what we rely on.
